video_title: Annie Lamont: $14B Managed, 70+ Exits, 15 IPOs, 7x Midas Investor
gist: Oak HC/FT co-founder Annie Lamont argues AI has, in the last two years, finally made drug discovery productive (Chai Discovery ~100x antibody productivity, roadmap to peptides and small molecules) while warning China now captures ~50% of pharma's outside R&D spend. She calls Devoted Health the world's best AI-in-healthcare example (tripled size, rising EBITDA), sees broadening healthcare exits to labs and big tech, and thinks only ~10% of richly valued AI companies justify their prices.

insights.claim: Annie Lamont says Oak HC/FT watched AI in life sciences for a decade without it producing more developable therapeutics, but that this changed decisively in the last two years.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: A seasoned healthcare VC is signalling AI-bio has crossed from hype to real productivity; capital flows into the space should accelerate.
insights.quote: we've been looking at AI for the last decade and have had not seen it produce more developable products and therapeutics. Uh, and everything's changed the last two years.

insights.claim: Oak HC/FT is deliberately deepening its life-sciences AI exposure, adding partners and expanding its San Francisco office because most AI development, including for life sciences, is happening in San Francisco.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Even sector-specialist East Coast funds are relocating talent to SF to stay close to AI model builders.

insights.claim: The current AI-bio wave rests on purpose-built biological and chemistry models (not LLMs) plus physical AI and lab robotics, enabled by the infrastructure that grew up around LLMs.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Investable picks are domain-specific foundation models and lab automation, not generic LLM wrappers.
insights.quote: You've created biological models and models around chemistry that are not LLMs.

insights.claim: Lamont frames drug development as the most expensive, most haphazard industry with the highest failure ratio, so even modest AI-driven improvements in odds of success and speed are game-changing.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Value capture in AI-bio comes from raising probability of success, which compounds across a pipeline.

insights.claim: Chai Discovery's AI tools make antibody design roughly 100x more productive than a lab without them, according to Lamont.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: If true, wet-lab-heavy discovery CROs and in-house discovery teams face severe productivity pressure.
insights.quote: like a hundred times more productive than a lab without them.

insights.claim: Chai Discovery's roadmap runs antibodies first (already being nailed), then peptides (material progress but not yet shown to customers), then small molecules.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Watch for Chai peptide product launches as the next milestone; small molecules is the later, larger battleground.

insights.claim: Lamont predicts Chai Discovery will soon have a majority of the largest pharmaceutical companies working with it in a deep way and could become 'a company for the ages' owning a large piece of the drug design continuum.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Chai is positioning as platform infrastructure for pharma R&D; signals rapid enterprise adoption by top pharma.
insights.quote: this may be a company for the ages.

insights.claim: Chai's defensibility comes from a data-driven moat: its models are evolving faster than anyone else's because of the data it works with, which Lamont sees as the sign of a differentiated, durable AI company.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Diligence test for AI companies: is model improvement rate outpacing competitors due to proprietary data loops?

insights.claim: Chai is building products, not just models, usable by non-tech-savvy pharma staff to design new drugs and improve existing ones, and every step from discovery through clinical trials can be redesigned via simulation validated against wet-lab and animal models.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Product usability by non-technical pharma scientists is the adoption lever; reformulation of existing drugs is an extra revenue lane.

insights.claim: Lamont says the biggest impact of AI in healthcare will probably be in life sciences and drug creation rather than payer/provider markets.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Implies relative overweighting of AI-bio versus AI-provider/admin plays for healthcare-focused investors.

themes.theme: China's biotech threat to US pharma

insights.claim: Lamont says that in the last four years roughly 50% of the outside research dollars big pharma spends now go to China, which was not the case five years ago.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: A massive shift of pharma external R&D/licensing to China; US biotech faces pricing and competition pressure.
insights.quote: pharma in the last four years has 50% of the outside dollars they're spending on research are going to China.

insights.claim: Lamont calls China's life-sciences trajectory 'wildly threatening' and an existential threat to the US pharma and biotech industry, requiring technology, investment and a complete re-engineering of the FDA and its processes to fix rapidly.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Expect policy pressure on FDA reform and China licensing; AI tools that speed US development are framed as strategic.
insights.quote: we have an existential threat in this country

insights.claim: Contrary to the narrative that China only makes me-too drugs, Lamont says Chinese universities and research arms now produce as many or more patents than the US, even though many Chinese drugs are slight modifications re-introduced to the US.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Discounting Chinese biotech as copycat is outdated; Chinese-originated assets will keep flowing into Western pipelines.

insights.claim: Lamont warns that NIH pulling research funding and undermining grants and international researchers at US universities will compromise the future US drug pipeline, though it is not yet a problem today.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Lagged risk to US early-stage innovation supply; may push more pharma sourcing toward China over time.

insights.claim: COVID exposed the danger of China producing about 90% of ingredients for antibiotics, a supply-chain dependency Lamont flags as a national risk.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Supports onshoring of API manufacturing as a policy-backed theme.

insights.claim: Lamont calls Devoted Health probably the best example of AI applied to healthcare in the world right now, noting she is not usually hyperbolic.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: A top healthcare VC's highest-conviction AI healthcare holding; benchmark for integrated payer-provider models.
insights.quote: probably the best example of AI applied to healthcare in the world right now.

insights.claim: Over the last year Devoted Health tripled its size, improved its operating ratio and dramatically increased its EBITDA, per Lamont.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Devoted is scaling profitably; a likely large IPO candidate and a competitive threat to Medicare Advantage incumbents.
insights.quote: Over the last year, they've tripled the size of their company.

insights.claim: Devoted's moat comes from slow, capital-intensive building blocks: state-by-state licensing, provider networks in every state, broker and member go-to-market, a proprietary payer tech platform, and its own Devoted Medical Group primary-care network owning risk and the member.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Scaling speed matters less than defensibility; vertically integrated MA plans with owned tech are hard for Blues and incumbents to match.

insights.claim: Lamont says Devoted Health will be almost impossible to compete against and will move into the commercial insurance market in the future.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Commercial-market entry would expand Devoted's TAM well beyond Medicare Advantage and pressure commercial payers.

insights.claim: The ideal healthcare model is a proactive virtual overlay with an AI front end and a doctor behind the AI, combined with a seamless insurer and member experience, which Devoted embodies.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Template for evaluating next-gen payer/provider startups.

themes.theme: AI in care delivery and admin cost

insights.claim: Lamont believes hospital systems and acute-care providers are not going anywhere, but are at the very beginning of an AI-assisted transformation that removes administrative burden from clinicians.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Disruption in provider markets is augmentation, not displacement; sell-to-hospitals AI admin tools have a long runway.

insights.claim: Administrative costs account for 25 to 30% of all healthcare costs, making them the prime target for AI-driven cost reduction, according to Lamont.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Admin automation (scribing, revenue cycle, prior auth) addresses a very large cost pool.
insights.quote: 25 to 30% of all health care costs are really administrative.

insights.claim: Electronic health records were the great organizing principle for data that AI can now use, making AI the first technology to actually take burden off clinicians.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: EHR incumbents hold the data layer AI builds on; integration access is strategic.

insights.claim: Lamont cites that 30% of radiology images are read wrong or have something missed, and argues AI backing radiologists will mean little is missed, while more radiologists, not fewer, are probably needed.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: AI radiology is an augmentation market; demand for radiologists persists.
insights.quote: 30% of images are read wrong by radiologists

insights.claim: Vision models and robotics will let surgeons see and manipulate better than today, making Da Vinci look like brute force by comparison, and could enable remote direction of surgery to close rural outcome gaps.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Next-gen surgical robotics with AI vision may challenge Intuitive's incumbency; remote surgery addresses rural access.
insights.quote: Da Vinci was a a brute forcing almost compared to what we're going to see now.

insights.claim: Lamont says the healthcare exit landscape is broadening: beyond the McKessons, Cardinals and roughly five payers that historically bought companies, frontier AI labs and large tech firms may now acquire healthcare software assets.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: More strategic buyers means higher exit multiples for healthcare AI software than historical PE-driven exits.

insights.claim: Lamont cites Microsoft's Nuance acquisition and Oracle's Cerner acquisition as precedents and suggests big tech could go broader and deeper into healthcare.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Big tech remains a plausible acquirer class for healthcare AI.

insights.claim: Highly valued incumbents will lack embedded expertise and talent to build new AI companies and will have to buy them to keep expanding TAM.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Supports a buy-not-build exit thesis for AI startups.

insights.claim: Carebridge, founded by Brad Smith with Oak, is the most recent great healthcare M&A example: sold to Elevance, it is working extremely well and being dramatically expanded inside the acquirer.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Elevance is an active, effective acquirer of care-delivery platforms.

insights.claim: Lamont says there are probably more M&A failures than successes, and success depends on whether the acquirer retains and empowers talent; she contrasts JPMorgan, which elevated the best people from acquisitions, with Credit Suisse, which prioritized incumbents and disrespected acquired talent.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Assess acquirers by culture: strategic talent integration versus political empire-building.

insights.claim: Lamont estimates only about 5-10% of companies receiving $1B-$20B valuations are worth them; most lack a large enough TAM and won't exceed $1-2B in value, and the current distortion will correct as it always does.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Expect a valuation correction for niche AI apps; be selective on late-stage entries.
insights.quote: I just think you've got 10% of them of the world it's worth it and 90% it's not.

insights.claim: Niche AI companies, such as AI applied to TPA software, will ultimately be bought on EBITDA multiples rather than strategic multiples, whereas Oak has historically sold companies at roughly a 30% strategic premium.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: AI label alone does not earn a strategic multiple; exit buyers for vertical niche software are PE-style.
insights.quote: They're they're going to buy it on ibida

insights.claim: Lamont sees huge runways in enterprise tech/ERP (e.g., Rillet), pharma (Chai) and some healthcare AI like Ambience, versus many niche companies with capped size.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Large-TAM AI categories: ERP, pharma R&D, clinical documentation.

insights.claim: Lamont says AI is the most interesting and seminal change in her 30-plus years of investing, realigning the entire economy, and fundamentally different from the 2021 digital-economy bubble.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Veteran investor sees AI as structural, not cyclical, despite expecting valuation froth to correct.

themes.theme: Oak HC/FT fund strategy and new bets

insights.claim: Oak HC/FT grew from a $500M first fund to $2B in each of its last two funds, driven by more opportunities and higher capital needs of today's companies.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Healthcare/fintech specialist scaling to multi-stage platform size.

insights.claim: Oak operates as a life-cycle investor writing $1M to $100M checks, sometimes committing $100M from day one, keeping 20-40% of a fund ($400M-$800M) in early stage, and can put up to 10% of a fund into public stocks such as biotech PIPEs.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Barbell-capable firm can buy early before valuations run and keep reserves to stay material in growth rounds.

insights.claim: Lamont describes a barbell venture market: seed and early funds on one side and returning very-late-stage and crossover money on the other, where a firm must write large checks to matter to entrepreneurs.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Mid-sized funds risk irrelevance; scale or specialization is required.

insights.claim: In life sciences, going public is often a funding mechanism rather than a liquidity event, and public-company investing can give proprietary information, making biotech PIPEs attractive to Oak.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Expect crossover/venture-style PIPE activity in AI-enabled biotech.

insights.claim: Fintech and healthcare together represent roughly 50% of the economy, and healthcare is 'the smallest large market' (about 100 providers that matter and 10 large payers), so Oak's buyer relationships help horizontal AI companies sell into it.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Distribution into concentrated healthcare buyers is a moat that sector-specialist VCs can monetize in AI.
insights.quote: it's the smallest large market you've ever seen

insights.claim: Augur, founded by former Amazon supply-chain and e-commerce chief Dave Clark, builds an AI orchestration, data-insights and agent execution layer for supply chain and logistics, already serving Fortune 500 clients with real revenue in its second year; Oak committed $100M up front.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Agentic supply-chain software is a funded, large-check category with a marquee operator founder.
insights.quote: we committed $100 million to them up front.

insights.claim: Lamont says COVID revealed that major companies' supply-chain software and analytics were far less sophisticated than assumed and could not adapt to change, creating demand for real-time analytics plus agents that act immediately.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Enterprise supply-chain modernization remains an underpenetrated AI market.

insights.claim: Illuminate, an Oak core position, builds reinforcement-learning environments for frontier labs that simulate financial analyst workflows (models, investment summaries, scorecards, legal work) and even an entire real estate brokerage, and went from zero to 60 in six months.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: RL environment vendors selling to labs are a fast-growing picks-and-shovels category; finance domain is a wedge.

insights.claim: About 15% of Oak's activity is company creation or buildups from the idea stage, including Augur, Curano in value-based care, and ambulatory infusion center roll-outs.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Incubation and buy-and-build in services is a meaningful part of Oak's strategy.

themes.theme: Founder selection in the AI era

insights.claim: Lamont argues that because the rate of change is so fast, the bar for founders has risen: many more backed entrepreneurs must be near top-percentile caliber to compete with the flood of new, well-funded companies.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Founder quality concentration drives returns; mediocre teams get squeezed faster.

insights.claim: Contrary to claims that companies won't need engineers, Lamont sees first-wave AI winners as product- and tech-oriented founders (computer science backgrounds) learning a new market, so diligence focuses on whether they grasp go-to-market and are humble enough to hire around gaps.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Back technical founders entering verticals, then test their GTM humility.

insights.claim: Brad Smith's success across three Oak-backed companies came from building models nobody else was doing, in contrast to the many me-too healthcare startups that once kept Oak away from Silicon Valley.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: Originality of model, not crowded categories, predicts healthcare startup outcomes.

insights.claim: Early mentor Jerry Gallagher told Lamont her bar for entrepreneurs was not high enough, a lesson that shifted her from thesis- and numbers-driven investing to people-first investing.
insights.speaker: Annie Lamont
insights.so_what: People-first underwriting outlasts thesis-first or metric-chasing.
insights.quote: the bar for your entrepreneurs is not high enough
